new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word is accented on its first syllable (a monosyllable on its only syllable). Within a phrase (the stretch between two junctures) the first word's first syllable carries primary stress and the first syllable of each following word carries secondary stress; all other syllables are unaccented. Stress is thus predictable and non-contrastive, and word boundaries are marked only by it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress accent on the first syllable of every non-initial word of a phrase; weaker than the primary and often hard to distinguish from either primary stress or no stress. No rhythmic secondary stress within the word is mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphophonemic rules on pp. 18–19 refer to the accent: '3. In syllables with secondary accent or no accent, (a) ey > iy and ay > ey > iy, and, no matter what the accent, (b) iy >..'; '10. In an unaccented syllable a short vowel preceding r disappears'; and a noun 'in certain constructions.. loses its accent (becomes suffixal; the full word and the suffixal..)', i.e. an encliticized noun is unaccented.
new_statements.identity_note: Emeneau's Kota is the language of the Nilgiri Hills Kota villages (Kolme:l and others) recorded 1935–1938; no dialect split is stated in the passages read. Krishnamurti's book, if it discusses Kota stress, would be reporting Emeneau's data, not new fieldwork.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog (gordon: Kota initial, initial stress) and with both existing statements held by the project (which are this same passage): word stress fixed on the first syllable; adds the phrase-level primary/secondary distribution, the weakness of the accent relative to English, vowel reductions in non-primary syllables, and de-accented enclitic/suffixal forms. new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word is stressed on its first syllable (monosyllables on their only syllable). Within a phrase (the stretch between two pauses/terminal contours) the first word's initial syllable carries primary stress and the initial syllable of every following word carries secondary stress; all other syllables are unstressed. Stress is thus non-contrastive and demarcative: word boundaries were established from phrase-initial/final occurrences.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Phrase-level only: the first syllable of each non-initial word in a phrase has secondary stress accent ('less strong than the primary' per the FTS snippets); no word-internal rhythmic secondary stress is described. Rule 3 (p. 18): in syllables with secondary accent or no accent ey > iy, ay > ey > iy in allegro speech.
new_statements.exceptions: irl 'night' after another noun in certain constructions 'loses its accent (becomes suffixal..) and the vowel disappears; e.g., odrlk "for one night"' (rule 11, p. 19); the quotative verb in-, id- 'say' has a suffixal form -n-, -d- 'having no accent' (sect. 12, p. 19), otherwise it carries a secondary accent; proper names written without word division 'though many of them have more than one accent' (p. 19); a phrase like ma mu'l is shown by its accent (' ma mu'l) to be two words (text note p. 30).
new_statements.identity_note: Emeneau 1944 describes the Kota of the Nilgiri Hills (Tamil Nadu) as dictated 1936-38 chiefly by one informant from Kolme·l village (per held introduction fragments), i.e. the language of Glottolog kota1263; Krishnamurti 2003 lists Kota as language 10 of South Dravidian I with Emeneau 1944-6 as its source, so his coverage of Kota is derivative of Emeneau.

new_statements.quote: There is no phonemic stress in any of the Dravidian languages. Normally stress (loudness) falls on the initial syllable of a word, short or long. A non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's initial-stress coding and with Emeneau 1944: initial prominence, explicitly non-phonemic, weight-independent ('short or long'); it is a family-level generalisation (Krishnamurti's Kota source is Emeneau 1944-6), not an independent Kota description.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement covering Kota among the 26 Dravidian languages: stress is not phonemic anywhere in Dravidian; phonetic prominence (loudness) normally falls on the word-initial syllable regardless of its weight, with non-initial long vowels louder than short vowels. No Kota-specific stress rule is given in the parts seen.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated; only 'a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels' (p. 27).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kota. (Sec. 2.4.1 snippets report deviations only for Telugu perception tests p. 60 and a Konda dialect p. 161.)
